title: N+1, SELECT_IN, JOINED — pick correctly and explain
description: Three short scenarios from the lesson. For each, choose the right loading strategy and explain why in your own words.

questions.prompt: You load 10 articles with em.find(Article, {}) and then access article.tags inside a forEach. The log shows 11 SELECTs. What is the diagnosis?

options.label: Classic N+1 — 1 SELECT for the articles + 1 SELECT per article to lazy-load tags.
The Identity Map cleared itself between iterations.
The connection pool is too small.

questions.rubric: Name the lazy-collection access in the loop and the fix: populate: ['tags'] or em.populate after find.

questions.prompt: You need articles with their tags (M:M). Articles: 100. Average tags per article: 5. You want fewest bytes on the wire. Pick the strategy.

options.label: SELECT_IN — one SELECT for articles, one SELECT IN (...) for tags.
JOINED — single round-trip via LEFT JOIN.
Leave it lazy — let each article load its own tags.
Drop to raw SQL via qb.execute().

questions.rubric: Strong answers mention that JOINED produces a cartesian-style row explosion (100 x 5 = 500 rows with duplicated article columns); SELECT_IN stays at 100 + 500 deduplicated rows and lets MikroORM hydrate cleanly.

questions.prompt: You load 1 article with its single author (1:1 / M:1). One row total. Pick the strategy.

options.label: JOINED — one SELECT with a LEFT JOIN, no extra round-trip.
SELECT_IN — two queries to avoid joins.
It does not matter for one entity.

questions.rubric: Reasoning should be: to-one relations don't cause row duplication. One round-trip beats two whenever the JOIN is cheap.

modelAnswer: Rule of thumb from the lesson: to-one relations (M:1, 1:1) favor JOINED — no row explosion. To-many relations (1:M, M:M) favor SELECT_IN — avoids the cartesian blow-up. N+1 happens whenever you touch a lazy collection inside a loop without populate; the fix is populate or em.populate(entities, [...]) before the loop.

title: Order the steps to diagnose and fix N+1
description: You spot an N+1 in production logs. Put the diagnostic + fix steps in the correct order, from first observation to verified fix.

widgetConfig.prompt: Order these steps from first action (spotting the symptom) to last (confirming the fix). Six steps, one correct order.

steps.label: 1. Spot the symptom: query log shows 1 SELECT for the parent rows followed by N tiny SELECTs.
steps.detail: Each tiny SELECT looks like `WHERE parent_id = $1 LIMIT $2` repeated.

steps.label: 2. Locate the trigger: find the loop or .map that touches the lazy collection.
3. Choose strategy: populate + SELECT_IN for to-many, populate + JOINED for to-one.
4. Apply populate: ['relation'] on the em.find call (or em.populate before the loop).
5. Rerun with debug:true and confirm exactly 2 SELECTs total (parent + IN(...)).
6. Add a test or assertion on query count so the regression cannot sneak back.

modelAnswer: Spot the symptom in the log -> locate the lazy access in code -> pick a strategy based on cardinality -> apply populate -> rerun and verify query count -> guard against regression with a test. Skipping the last step is how N+1 reappears one refactor later.

title: Break partial loading on purpose — plan, observe, fix (AI-resilient)
description:
Break partial loading on purpose, then fix it, and ship both states as a PR. Query Articles with fields: ['title', 'author.name'] WITHOUT the FK column (authorId) and observe what article.author becomes. Then fix it by adding 'author' (the relation property name) or 'authorId' to the fields array.

In the PR description, include: (1) a 2-sentence up-front prediction — proxy, undefined, or fully-loaded Author? (2) both the broken and fixed query logs (copy-paste); (3) a revision note — was your prediction right, what does this tell you about how MikroORM resolves relations from a partial result set, and when this bug is silent (no runtime error) but produces wrong data.

Commit the broken version and the fix as separate commits if you can. Submit the link to your branch or PR.
modelAnswer: Without the FK column in the partial-load fields, MikroORM cannot reconstruct the relation — article.author ends up undefined or a half-empty proxy depending on the path. The broken log shows a SELECT that omits author_id; the fixed one includes it. The silent-bug case: when the rest of the code defensively checks `if (article.author)` and silently skips it. AI answers usually say 'include the FK in fields' but don't warn about the silent-skip pattern that hides the data corruption from your test suite.
